name: Militarism
summary: Militarism holds that war is a permanent and even ennobling feature of relations between states, that a state's highest end is power, and that the armed forces and martial virtues (obedience, duty, self-sacrifice) deserve primacy in state and society. Its classical theorists rejected arbitration, disarmament and the peace movement, defended conquest and colonies as the right of the stronger, and wanted universal service, a military-minded education and a government or monarch above parliamentary politics. Scholars such as Vagts distinguish it from the ordinary 'military way' of preparing for war under civilian direction.
scope: The name itself, as the defining sources (Britannica, EBSCO Research Starters, the 1914-1918-online encyclopedia article, the Gale encyclopedia entry, Mann, Samotin's survey) define it: prioritizing military strength, values and methods over civilian ones, with classical Prussian-German militarism as the case they name (Treitschke and Bernhardi, 'representative of a general view that war was natural and right') and Japan 1931-45 as the other. Texts: Bernhardi's Germany and the Next War, Treitschke's Politics lectures, the 1882 Rescript to Soldiers and Sailors, and the IMTFE judgment as the record of Japan. Excludes Ludendorff, Moltke and Songun/North Korea, whose texts no defining source ties to militarism (Songun is its own subject), and military rule, fascism and nationalism.

notes: Rules-7 pass (2026-11-20): answers resting on inference, on a general value, on strand splits that needed Ludendorff, Moltke or Songun, or on one strand's silence were nulled; Ludendorff (s4), Moltke (s5), Songun (s7, s8) and Wikipedia (s11) remain listed only because the reviewHistory of the nulled answers cites them, and no current answer does. Japan's record (s6, IMTFE) answers alone where cited. Themes searched: world, means, government, society and economy statements; militarism's defining sources describe an attitude toward war and the military, so economy, culture, ecology and technology stay null. Kokutai no Hongi and Vagts could not be read in full online.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Treitschke calls protection of citizens by arms the first and essential task of the state, and Britannica defines militarism as prioritizing military strength.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: Treitschke holds that the state must enforce obedience to its laws whether willingly or not; abolishing coercive institutions is the opposite.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: Bernhardi states that in the clash of nations it is not the possessor but the victor who has the right, so conquest settles title.

arbitrator-settles-disputes.rationale: Bernhardi argues arbitration courts are impractical and detrimental to an expanding people and cannot render war impossible.

arms-reduction.rationale: Bernhardi treats disarmament and peace schemes as harmful to a rising nation and wants armaments expanded; Treitschke scorns the blind worshippers of perpetual peace.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Bernhardi writes that higher civilization and the greater power that goes with it are the foundation of the right to annexation and subjugation.

class-collaboration.rationale: Bernhardi wants workers reconciled with the existing state through social legislation and won back to national ideals.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Bernhardi and Treitschke see history as driven by the rivalry and wars of states, and Bernhardi wants the working class won back to state and nation.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: Bernhardi presents colonies as a necessity for German power and growth, and Treitschke wants a colony won in the next successful war; colonies serve the metropole's strength.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Bernhardi presents the struggle for existence as a law of nature that war carries into the life of nations; Treitschke says brave nations thrive and weak ones rightly go to the wall.

conscription.rationale: Bernhardi praises universal military service as the clearest expression of the idea of the State and wants it fully applied.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Treitschke writes that citizens' inward consent is not absolutely necessary and that kingdoms have lasted for centuries without it.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Bernhardi calls Germany the greatest civilized people in history, and Treitschke says weak and cowardly nations go to the wall and rightly so.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: Bernhardi blames internationalist social-democratic agitation for weakening the nation and wants workers devoted to the national state in war.

democracy-best.rationale: Bernhardi writes that no people is so little suited as the Germans to parliamentary or republican government, and Treitschke upholds a strong monarchy; the Gale entry notes militarism also appears inside democracies, so the stance is disagreement rather than total rejection.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Treitschke writes that history wears masculine features and is not for women, and attacks the emancipation of women.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Bernhardi says that in war the individual disappears before the conception of the state and must sacrifice himself for the community.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Treitschke treats hereditary succession as a condition of real monarchy, which he holds the best form of state.

elective-rulers.rationale: Treitschke treats hereditary succession as a condition of monarchy, which he holds the best form of state.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Bernhardi calls arbitration courts and peace treaties futile and harmful to a rising nation, and Treitschke says no judge above sovereign states can even be imagined.

force-without-un.rationale: Bernhardi rejects arbitration and any outside authority over a nation's decision for war, so approval by an international body is not needed.

individual-rights-only.rationale: Bernhardi makes the nation and state the bearer of right and duty, with the individual disappearing before the conception of the state.

initiating-nondefensive-force-unjustifie.rationale: Bernhardi justifies war for expansion and conquest, calling it a biological necessity and a moral obligation, not only defence.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Treitschke sees history as made by the wars and rivalry of states and great men, not by economic structure.

military-force-beyond-defence.rationale: Britannica says militarism holds that a country should use its military forces extensively, including gunboat diplomacy; Bernhardi defends war for expansion and power, extolling the use of force in international politics in the 1914-1918-online article's words.

military-superiority.rationale: Bernhardi argues Germany must build forces able to defeat its rivals rather than merely deter them, and Britannica defines militarism as a nation prioritizing military strength to gain power.

nation-first.rationale: Bernhardi writes that the end-all and be-all of a state is power, and Treitschke that the state's first duty is to maintain itself; neither admits a duty of global cooperation above national interest.

national-law-over-international.rationale: Bernhardi argues no self-respecting nation would sacrifice its own conception of right to a universal international law.

national-self-determination.rationale: Treitschke says weak nations rightly perish and Bernhardi that the victor has the right, so no nation has a right to its own state merely by being a nation.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: Treitschke praises the moral majesty of war and holds that the state's first task is protection by arms; absolute non-violence is the opposite.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Treitschke says the state demands obedience and its laws must be kept whether willingly or not.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: Bernhardi praises a German government that stands above all parties, and Treitschke prizes the monarchy as the unifying national tradition.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Bernhardi writes that no people is so little suited as the Germans to parliamentary or republican government and mocks the Reichstag; Treitschke wants a constitutional monarchy that keeps the kingship strong.

patriotic-education.rationale: The IMTFE judgment records that military training became compulsory throughout Japan's school system by 1927 and that school textbooks dealt with Japanese military history.

people-in-arms.rationale: Bernhardi wants universal service built around a trained standing army and officer corps, and Kamman notes the officer caste's central place; a militia replacing the professional army was a liberal and socialist demand.

person-over-state.rationale: Bernhardi subordinates the individual wholly to the state's power and survival: the individual must forget his egoism and his life is nothing in comparison with the community.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Treitschke calls the dream of a world state irrational and treats sovereignty, the power to declare war when it chooses, as essential to a state.

recognize-territorial-claims-from-conque.rationale: Bernhardi: the right of conquest by war has always been admitted, and 'it is not the possessor, but the victor, who then has the right'.

state-harmful.rationale: Treitschke defines the state as the public power of offence and defence and writes that without war there would be no state, so the state is the precondition of everything militarists value.

suppress-opposition.rationale: The IMTFE judgment records that Japan's militarists set out to crush the political parties and that the Army exercised censorship of its own from 1931.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Bernhardi holds that growing nations need new territory and that the victor, not the possessor, has the right; Treitschke writes that states expand mostly by conquest.

uniformed-youth.rationale: The IMTFE judgment records compulsory military drill in Japan's schools and youth schools for ages seventeen to twenty-one, inspected by the War Ministry.

universal-morality.rationale: Bernhardi argues Christian morality is personal and cannot govern states, and that each nation has its own conception of right.

war-builds-character.rationale: Treitschke calls war the mightiest moulder of nations and Bernhardi says war is a biological necessity and that the possibility of war gives a nation's character its stimulus; the 1914-1918-online article describes Bernhardi as extolling the use of force in international politics.

women-suffrage.rationale: Treitschke mocks experiments with female suffrage and attacks the emancipation of women.

workers-nation.rationale: Bernhardi attacks international social democracy as hostile to the national state and wants workers won back to the ideals of country.
